title: Talking to Strangers on the Train
text:
Every morning, commuters in Chicago sit side by side on trains and buses in near total silence. Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder of the University of Chicago wondered whether this silence was really what people wanted.

In 2014 they published a set of field experiments. Researchers approached commuters on the platform and gave them one of three instructions: strike up a conversation with a stranger on the ride, keep to yourself, or commute as you normally would. Each person got a sealed survey to fill in at the end of the ride and mail back.

Those who had talked to a stranger reported the most pleasant commute, and they did not report getting less done. Yet when other commuters were asked to predict how each condition would feel, they expected the opposite: talking to a stranger would be the least pleasant option. Many believed others would not want to talk to them. The researchers found similar results with taxi passengers and in the lab, where people underestimated how interested strangers would be in talking. The silence on the train was not a shared preference, but a shared mistake that kept everyone apart.
lesson: Most strangers are more open to a friendly word than you expect. Next time you sit next to someone, try a short conversation; you will probably both enjoy it.
source: Epley, N., and Schroeder, J. (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980-1999.
